Scientific progress often begins with a deceptively simple question. Before reaching for a complex model, it helps to understand which assumptions are doing the real work.
A good model is not necessarily the most complicated one. It is the one that helps us understand something meaningful about the world.

title: 2D projection of 3D world
text:
Start with the question
Consider a simple linear relationship between an input (x) and an observed response (y):
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \epsilon
\]
Here, (_0) represents the intercept, (_1) the slope, and () the part of the observation that the model does not explain.
This simple equation already encodes assumptions about how the variables relate to one another. Understanding those assumptions is often more valuable than immediately reaching for a more elaborate model.

title: 2D projection of 3D world
text:
A small computational experiment
We can explore the relationship with a few lines of Python:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
y = 2 * x + 1

plt.plot(x, y, color="#47745b", linewidth=2)
plt.xlabel("Input")
plt.ylabel("Predicted response")
plt.show()
The code is intentionally simple. It produces a straight line, but it also gives us a starting point for thinking about noise, uncertainty, and the limitations of our assumptions.

title: 2D projection of 3D world
text:
What simplicity really means
Simplicity is not the absence of detail. It is the deliberate choice of which details matter.
In scientific work, a useful explanation should make its reasoning inspectable. Equations should clarify the argument, figures should reveal patterns, and code should make computational claims easier to reproduce.
The goal is not to make every problem simple. It is to understand what makes a problem difficult before deciding how to solve it.
